--- title: "Anthropogenic heat and air-conditioner adoption in Greater Mumbai" pagetitle: "Overview" subtitle: "A bottom-up urban building energy model coupled to a household agent-based model" --- ::: {.hero} Every air conditioner moves heat from inside a building to the street. As Mumbai's households buy them, the city's waste heat rises — and the households least able to afford cooling live in the dwellings that get hottest. This project quantifies both halves of that sentence for all 580,890 buildings inside the 24 BMC wards. ::: [The visual story](index.html){.story-link}   [Explore the map](map/index.html){.story-link} ::: {#a01fe49f .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## What this is Two models, coupled. **A bottom-up urban building energy model.** Building footprints and heights become a stock of typed archetypes. Each carries an appliance load and a cooling load driven by outdoor temperature, and each rejects waste heat to the street: base electricity roughly one-to-one, plus condenser heat of Q~cool~(1 + 1/COP). Human metabolism and road traffic are added, and the total is aggregated to a 100 m grid at hourly resolution. **An agent-based model of who buys an air conditioner.** Households are agents. Each year, every household without an AC decides whether to buy one, based on what it can afford, how hot its own dwelling gets, and how many of its neighbours already have one. Those that own one choose a setpoint and how long to run it. The resulting waste heat raises the city's temperature, which raises next year's discomfort — the loop that makes this an ABM rather than a projection. ## What it shows **The city-scale magnitude checks out.** Q~f~ over built cells comes to 20.58 W/m² against 23.5 W/m² from the published extrapolation for Mumbai, but peaks at 18:00 rather than 16:00. That two-hour gap is the substantive result: the benchmark's diurnal shape comes from US utility load curves, while Indian residential demand peaks in the evening. **Adoption roughly triples by 2040**, adding 3.2 W/m² of waste heat and 452 MW of peak demand, with no population growth or new construction in the model. **Thermal inequality is measurable and it runs the wrong way.** Informal dwellings sit 1.6 °C hotter on average and 4.0 °C hotter at peak than tower flats, carry 65% more discomfort degree-hours, and run cooling at 64% of the rate. The heat they are exposed to outdoors is produced largely by other people's machines. **The two mechanisms are separable.** Sensitivity screening puts affordability and the baseline purchase rate at the top and indoor discomfort near the bottom for adoption, while discomfort produces the largest spread across the stock. Income and price decide *who adopts*; building fabric decides *who suffers while not adopting*. ::: {.caveat} **This is an uncalibrated prototype.** The building physics and the agent logic are real; the behavioural coefficients are not fitted to observation, and the two that dominate the result have no empirical anchor. Treat trajectories as structural, not predictive. See [Limits](limitations.qmd). ::: ## Built in a day The whole pipeline — data assembly, energy model, thermal model, ABM, sensitivity screening, web map — was built in a single session on 19 September 2026, then paused for documentation. [Reproduce](reproduce.qmd) has the commands.
